What the small survey shows

A fictional class asked twenty learners how they reviewed new vocabulary. Twelve reported using flashcards, six reported writing example sentences, and two reported neither method. The survey allowed one main method per learner. Thus, the corresponding proportions were sixty, thirty and ten percent.

The chart shows that flashcards were the most frequently reported main method in this group. It does not show that flashcards caused better learning: the survey did not measure results. Nor can twenty responses describe every learner at the school. Some participants also said that their method changed before a test.

The class decided to use the chart as a starting point for discussion. A later study could ask about several methods and compare results over time. For now, the careful conclusion concerns reported habits in one small group.

Two blue bicycles

A fictional neighborhood blog claimed that two people named Alex, both riding blue bicycles, must be relatives. The post added that both people had arrived at a repair shop on the same morning. Readers shared the story as an astonishing family coincidence.

The shop's records supported only part of the account. Two customers called Alex had appointments that day, but one bicycle was green. Neither customer had given evidence of a family connection. In addition, the shop had offered a discounted repair session that morning, which explained why several cyclists arrived together.

A careful summary retains the two shared names and the date, corrects the color claim and leaves the family relationship unconfirmed. Missing proof of a relationship does not by itself prove that the two customers were unrelated. It means that the original post went further than the available evidence.

The Self-Driving Car Artificial intelligence is clearly revolutionizing our world in many areas, and that includes transportation. In 2015, the installation rate of AI-based systems in new vehicles was 8%. This consisted mainly of speech-recognition systems. However, this rate is forecast to rise to 109% in 2025 due to the inclusion of multiple AI systems such as gesture controls, eye tracking, driver monitoring systems, and virtual assistants, among others. This will inevitably lead to a self-driving car, but opinions are divided as to whether autonomous cars are a good idea. Supporters of AI point to the fact that the vast majority of accidents are caused by human error such as drunk driving, speeding, tiredness, and a more recent phenomenon, distraction. Clearly, automated vehicles would eliminate all accidents of these kinds. They also argue that apart from the obvious benefit of protecting lives, fewer accidents would also save governments millions of dollars a year. Detractors argue that millions of workers actually make a living from transporting goods and people. The majority of these people would need to be reemployed. As for safety, if a child suddenly walked in front of a speeding car, what would happen? Would the car hit them or swerve off the road? Such a complex moral decision would have to be programmed into the machine. And if there were an accident, who would be responsible and who would pay for damages? Finally, some people actually enjoy driving, and if all vehicles were automated then they would be deprived of their hobby. Whatever your view, the automobile industry is not waiting, and many car companies plan to release models with driverless features in the near future. Then it's only a question of time before fully autonomous vehicles follow the trend. Whether the public accepts them, that's another question.

AI in Sports When most people think about artificial intelligence, they think about AI being applied to work or home life, but the sports world is being revolutionized by AI technology. Using wearable technology, data can be collected while players are performing. This provides many benefits. Finding Talent Using AI algorithms, sports teams can analyze a player's performance statistics in a single game, over their season, or throughout their career. Computers can analyze data faster than humans, providing a wealth of in-depth information that can be used to decide the next star that a team should recruit. Managing Health Using wearable technology, coaches can monitor players' heart rates and movements. In 2016, the soccer team Leicester City, using wearable technology, won the English Premier League partly because they kept more players injury-free by optimizing training sessions and resting tired players. Improving Performance By tracking the players' movements in training, the data that is generated can be used to see which players are performing well. In baseball, AI can calculate the speed at which players throw the ball and swing the bat. In tennis, wearables can read movements for different types of shots. In American football training sessions, cameras in helmets can show exactly what the players can see – invaluable information for coaches. Creating profiles of successful performance makes it easier for coaches to replicate success because players have models to follow. AI isn't perfect, and a large supply of data must be gathered before interpretations are made. Regardless of how sophisticated AI tools become, humans are not likely to be replaced soon. One AI industry expert suggested that AI would mainly be used to challenge the beliefs and selections of talent scouts rather than to replace talent scouts completely. With the wearable devices market expected to exceed $51.5 billion by 2022, it is clear that successful teams will be those embracing technology.

Personality Tests in Job Interviews Personality tests are increasingly used by companies during the recruitment process because they can save a lot of time and money, especially when there are hundreds or thousands of applicants. Another reason is that employees change jobs every four of five years on average, so taking on the right person who is likely to stick around will also save the company time and resources. Personality tests minimize the risk. The candidates themselves are sometimes very nervous. However, they should not worry, as there are no right or wrong answers and the tests are almost always used in conjunction with face-to-face interviews. Employers are looking at your values, beliefs, and attitudes in order to see if you are suited to the role, will get along with colleagues, and will fit in with the company culture. Some people claim that you can do better on personality tests by anticipating what the desired qualities are for the given role. It is said that to prepare for the test you should research the company thoroughly, be clear on the role you are applying for, and understand the company's values. Companies sometimes get their top performing staff to complete the test and may look for candidates who have similar profiles. However, experts say you can't cheat the test, as some of the questions are specifically designed to identify inconsistent answers. The same questions may be repeated, but worded differently. Secondly, if you get the job, you may find yourself in a role which isn't suited to your true personality. If you're introverted and like working alone, there is no point saying you are a chatty person who works well in a team. So remember that a personality test is nothing to be afraid of, so do your research, be yourself, and good luck!

First Impressions Have you heard the expression "first impressions count" and wondered if it were true? How exactly does someone assess us in those first moments, and can we improve our chances of making a good first impression? Here's what I've discovered. A first impression happens in the blink of an eye as we take in physical appearance, often judging characteristics like attractiveness and trustworthiness. In the next few seconds, signals about personality and competence are picked up. Even though these impressions are based on generalizations, studies show that first impressions can be difficult to change even when we are presented with facts that conflict with them. All this means that we should make an effort to make the best first impression we can. As most communication happens on a nonverbal level, you should first consider how you present yourself – a polished appearance, good posture, and a warm smile. Eye contact has been proven to create attraction, but if you think it will transmit that you are sincere, think again. Liars are known to hold eye contact longer than those who are telling the truth. Second, people generally prefer others who are similar to themselves in appearance, personality, attitude, beliefs, and behavior. Try to mirror the other person and don't reveal strong differences in opinion too soon. Significant differences in the way we look and speak will probably negatively affect initial impressions, but having just one thing in common may lead to assumptions that a person is similar to us in many ways. Finally, make sure your handshake is firm, confident, and friendly. It's the first physical contact you will make, and its significance is often underestimated. So, now you know how to make a great first impression. Let other readers know your tips in the comments below.

A Strange Coincidence? I love a good coincidence, but I'm also a naturally skeptical person. Awkward Auditions You have finally got an audition to get a part in the play of your dreams. What could go wrong? Well, almost anything! We spoke to two actors who shared with us their most awkward audition moments so you can learn from their mistakes. Jack, 25 – I remember auditioning for a Shakespeare play, Hamlet. I had studied Hamlet at school, so I wasn't worried about the script, but I was concerned about getting the accent right, so I spent hours perfecting my English accent, listening to actors reading Shakespeare in sophisticated ways. When I started the audition, I said the first line, "To be or not to be …" and then my mind went blank. I couldn't remember the words. I should've invested more time in memorizing the text. Years later, I discovered that the original Shakespeare actors used a mix of local accents, so I had actually wasted my time trying to sound upper class! Since then, I memorize a script without fail and only use accents when instructed by the theater company. Mary, 27 – My audition consisted of a four-page scene and a song. I spent hours learning my lines, and I felt reasonably confident about the song. At the audition, my dialogue went pretty much as expected, but I put so much effort into it that I must have strained my voice. I didn't have any water with me and when I launched into my song, my mouth went dry - I just couldn't reach the higher notes! I sounded like a sick cat. It was horrible. Sadly, the audition ended there. I wanted to crawl under a rock! I ought to have done some light vocal exercises to warm up my voice beforehand. It's a lesson you only learn once! Post your experiences in the comments, please!

Thank you for your welcome. Today I'd like to talk about the importance of having a clear vision. I'll look at this from the standpoint of a business and also from the position of an individual. If a company has a clear vision, which is communicated to all members, then everyone is focused on the same outcome. It helps managers and staff pull together toward the same objectives. If there are any disagreements, then individuals can always come back to the overall vision to decide which is the most appropriate action to take. A vision is motivating as well because it is showing a future that is better. If staff know that they are working towards a future that benefits them, it is more likely they will work harder and overcome obstacles in their way. At this point, I'd like to stress the importance that a vision is communicated. If the employees have no idea of the management's vision, then it will have no effect on them at all. OK, let's move on. In your personal life, having a vision for your life is essential. If you don't, then it will be other people and circumstances that will direct your life for you. Modern life is full of distractions that keep people away from their purpose in life. One practical way you can keep your vision in front of you is to have a vision board. On this, you can put pictures of the house, car, or even the life of your dreams. Once you know your end point, you can start setting tangible goals. And finally, you must remember to take action! As Nelson Mandela said, "Vision without action is just a dream, action without vision just passes the time, and vision with action can change the world." Thank you.

Nanotechnology – The Size of Things to Come Nanotechnology is a branch of technology which deals with things on a very small scale, from 1 to 100 nanometers in size. How big is a nanometer? Well, 80,000 nanometers is about as wide as one human hair. The growth of nanotechnology was accelerated in 1981 with the invention of the atomic-resolution microscope, a microscope capable of viewing atoms more clearly than before. By 1989, scientists were able to manipulate atoms. Nanotechnology involves not only seeing but actually controlling the individual molecules and atoms that make up everything in the world, including you! This all might sound very theoretical, but in 2008, over 800 actual nanotech products were available, with more coming onto the market every week. If you are someone who often spills coffee on yourself, one company has created an unstainable shirt using a nanotechnology fabric that repels oils and water-based liquids. Two challenges for scientists are learning how to better manipulate molecules and atoms and to create nanorobots, tiny machines that can actually move inside our bodies. The latter is clearly a greater challenge, and at the time of writing, no artificial, non-biological nanorobots have been created. Possible uses for nanorobots would be in medicine where they could be put inside a patient to identify and remove harmful cells, such as cancer, or repair cells atom by atom. Another use for nanorobots is in cleaning up the environment. For example, when oil is spilled in the sea, nanorobots could change the properties of the oil to make it easier to pick up. At the moment, this is purely hypothetical, but with many companies and governments investing billions of dollars in nanotechnology, it may not be too long before humans, with the help of robots, might be able to clean up the planet.

Making It Big – In Micro-art Willard Wigan is a specialist in micro-sculpture. Not art the size of a mouse or an ant, Willard's sculptures are so small they can barely be seen by the human eye. He broke the Guinness World Record for the smallest work of art made by hand, a motorcycle he sculpted inside a single hair. He often displays his work inside the eye of a needle or on top of a pin head so the size can be appreciated. Visitors use microscopes to enjoy his works at exhibitions. At age five, Willard's first project was a house for ants. His mother saw it and encouraged him to make furniture for the ants. At school, Willard was struggling because he couldn't read, and he was treated badly by one teacher because he was quiet. As a means of escape, he channeled his energy into making small things. When he was 15, he purchased his first microscope and made tiny wooden sculptures. Since then, he has sculpted the White House on top of a pin and the Queen of England on a coffee bean. He has won awards and become a millionaire. Working with such small materials is not without its problems. Willard has to create an environment where nothing moves. Once a fly flew near one of his sculptures and blew away all his work. Another time a phone rang, causing Willard to inhale. He was working on a sculpture of Alice in Wonderland and the tiny figure of Alice disappeared up his nose! It is also mentally demanding work. He has trained himself to sculpt between heartbeats so his hand remains steady. Patience is also important, as one piece can take up to five weeks to complete, but with his sculptures selling for $50,000 or more, he isn't going to rush.

Working in Antarctica I will never forget traveling to the Concordia Research Station in Antarctica. The vast landscape is completely flat, and the base is about 370 miles away from any other facility. The average temperature is about –58°F, but can fall below –112°F, and the base is on a high plateau, which means less oxygen in the air. In fact, the environment is so harsh that you can only travel there and back within a three-month window each year. Most people on the base have two or three jobs, which stems from the fact that there are usually only about 13 people on the base. Duties include going outside every day to collect data for science projects. I was also responsible for cooking meals and dealing with dental emergencies. People think that only scientists work there, but we had a mechanic, a doctor, and an electrician. Apart from the work, I was also the subject of experiments. The lack of oxygen is of interest to scientists designing spaceships, since astronauts have less oxygen to breathe. They also investigate the possibility of living on other planets. Secondly, the base is so isolated that it's ideal for studies on solitude, which is valuable for those planning long space missions. I thought boredom would be the biggest problem, but this wasn't an issue because we had the internet and cell phones. In fact, facing extreme weather conditions every day was the biggest challenge – not only the freezing conditions, but the dangers presented by wind and, surprisingly, the brightness. Sunglasses were just as essential as warm clothes! Would I recommend it? Of course! It's challenging and monotonous work at times, but the experience of working in Antarctica is unique and rewarding, and the memories will last a lifetime.

How To Get the Remote Job of Your Dreams In recent years, the number of employees working mainly from home has increased dramatically. Employers love the benefits of increased productivity and lower costs. Workers love the flexibility and reduced travel time. Understandably, despite the increase in remote positions, competition for such jobs is high. So how can you make sure you ace the interview to get that remote job of your dreams? First, you have to be equipped with the latest computer systems and tools and be able to use them well. Communication will be via video conference, texts, and email. Show you can communicate effectively and concisely on these platforms. If you are not familiar with the tools of the trade, then you may be overlooked. Companies may hold interviews with such tools and will observe carefully how confidently you use them. They may also check how you interact on social media, so ensure your online presence will have a positive impact. Secondly, since you will be working unsupervised, you will need to show evidence that you can motivate yourself. In your interview, you should be ready to present examples of how you work productively alone. Employers will seek previous remote experience, so if you don't have it, get it. Look for freelance work or solo projects that show you can do amazing things by yourself. Finally, you need to be disciplined in managing your time. Make sure you bring to your interview examples of projects that show how you have coordinated your workload to meet deadlines. You might be asked how you prioritize tasks and manage distractions. Like any other interview, you should be informed about the company and the role. Sell yourself as the perfect candidate for the job rather than overselling the fact that you want to work remotely. Good luck, and share your experiences in the comments.

When boxer James "Buster" Douglas faced "Iron" Mike Tyson in Tokyo in February 1990, nobody expected anything except a Tyson victory. Some journalists didn't even bother traveling to Japan to report on the fight. Tyson was the undefeated heavyweight champion of the world, famous for destroying opponents with his powerful punches. His record of 37 wins included 34 knockouts, most of which were in the early rounds. His previous fight with Carl Williams ended in a knockout after just 93 seconds. Many people thought that the fight against Douglas, ranked seventh-best heavyweight, was just a warm-up for Tyson. It was the fight with Evander Holyfield, the next in line to fight Tyson, that people were excited about. Douglas did not have a happy lead up to the fight either. Three weeks before the fight, his mother died, and the day before the fight, he got the flu. Although Douglas was the underdog, he moved quickly when the fight started and took every opportunity to punch Tyson. But despite dominating the middle of the fight, Douglas was knocked down by Tyson in the last seconds of round eight. Douglas got up after a nine-second count. One second more and he would have lost. Instead, what he did was fight back in the ninth round and knock Tyson down in the tenth. Tyson, down for the first time in his career, could not get up before the referee had counted to ten, and the fight was over. Tyson wanted a rematch with Douglas, but Douglas refused, instead deciding to defend his title by fighting Holyfield. Having gained 15 pounds, Douglas was knocked out by Holyfield in the third round of their fight, and Douglas decided to retire soon after. Douglas' victory over Tyson is widely considered to be one of the biggest upsets in sports history.

The Science of Scary Are you one of those people who loves to be scared? Well, you're not alone. There are thousands of people who would rather watch a horror movie than a romantic comedy. But why are people attracted to entertainment that has them jumping out of their skins? First, we need to understand what fear is. Fear has been described as an emotional response induced by a perceived threat. It starts in a region of the brain called the amygdala, which detects things that stand out. For example, the sight of a bear would trigger a response in the amygdala and prepare the body to take action. It's an important emotion because if we didn't feel it, we wouldn't be able to respond to real dangers. So where does the enjoyment come in? Some people suggest that when we are afraid we are momentarily distracted from problems in our lives. Other experts say that the enjoyment is not from the fear itself, but from the feeling of tension being released after the fear has passed. It's important to highlight that two other parts of our brain, the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex, help us know whether a threat is real or not. A bear in the wild would produce a different reaction than a bear in a zoo. People watching a movie know it's not real, so they can experience the boost of adrenaline that comes from a scary scene knowing the physical reactions will wear off in time. If you are in the 10% of the population who gets a thrill from being scared, then you will be pleased to hear that horror movies are becoming more popular with Hollywood studios. They cost little to make, which makes them profitable, and they do well internationally because fear is a universal emotion.
